title: A `calls` edge may not name a PowerShell reserved word

exclusions.split: `$s.Split(…)` is a real .NET String method; the target of a `methodCall` edge is a member leaf. A first version of this instrument omitted the exclusions and reported 42 fabrications where 6 existed.
exclusions.contains: `$s.Contains(…)` and `$list.Contains(…)` are real .NET methods. The RESERVED-WORD sense (`-contains`) is an operator and never a command name.
exclusions.replace: `$s.Replace(…)` is a real .NET method; `-replace` is the operator form.
exclusions.match: `$s -match $re` and `$m = $s -match $re` are the OPERATOR, but a corpus can also write `$x.Match(…)`; the operator form is not a command and the method form is real, so the name cannot convict.

method: Candidates are the lane's production (non-test) .ps1/.psm1/.psd1 files under CORPUS_ROOT, drawn by a hash of the relative path so the sample is unbiased and reproducible. Each file goes through the PRODUCTION `parseFile` entry, so the worker-boundary relationship filter is included. Every `calls` edge whose target leaf is in the reserved set is reported with its file and line. The reserved set is a union of named PowerShell language references; names that are ALSO real .NET methods reachable as a member leaf are EXCLUDED with the reason recorded, because the first version of this instrument omitted the exclusions and reported 42 fabrications where 6 existed.
blindSpots: A reserved word the analyzer never reaches as a `command` is not measured, and a fabrication whose target happens to share a name with a real cmdlet is indistinguishable from a call. Both are bounds of a target-name census, declared rather than hidden.
